intro: Five themes moving drug development this week — an atopic-dermatitis target class edging toward a shared safety verdict, the incretin fight now in front of a judge, and access, approvals and capital all quietly renegotiating where the rules sit. Refreshed every Monday.

narratives.headline: OX40 in atopic dermatitis hardens from two failures into one safety question
narratives.detail: Two Phase 3-caliber programmes on the same costimulatory axis are gone in five months — Amgen's rocatinlimab (depleting anti-OX40) in March on a Kaposi's sarcoma signal, Sanofi's amlitelimab (anti-OX40L) in July on differentiation. Sanofi's fuller rationale now cites the "totality of efficacy and safety evidence" and reported Kaposi's sarcoma cases, with the phrasing ambiguous as to whether those cases sit in amlitelimab's own trials — which, if confirmed, would reframe the axis from two unrelated exits into one convergent target-class safety flag. Inmagene's non-depleting IMG-007 is the last clinical-stage asset standing, and its mechanism only answers the safety half of what sank the leaders.

narratives.headline: The incretin rivalry escalates from ad copy to the courtroom
narratives.detail: Novo Nordisk is seeking a New Jersey federal injunction against Lilly's comparative-efficacy campaigns pitting Zepbound and Mounjaro against Ozempic and Wegovy — the first time this fight has moved past press releases and marketing complaints into actual litigation. With the clinical race broadly settled on both sides, the contest is migrating to what the labels and the ads are allowed to say. The question worth watching is whether an injunction resets how incretin efficacy can be marketed at all.

narratives.headline: Approval stops being terminal — Amgen defends Tavneos before it's asked
narratives.detail: CHMP moved to revoke Tavneos (avacopan) in Europe in June, and Amgen is now proactively seeking an FDA advisory-committee hearing to defend the US approval ahead of any challenge. Set against CHMP's split rare-disease week — a positive opinion for Minoryx's ALD asset alongside a negative for Zevra's Meplyffa roughly two years after its US clearance — the pattern reads clearly on both sides of the Atlantic: a marketing authorization is increasingly a revisable state, not a finish line. Sponsors are starting to defend approvals they already hold.

narratives.headline: Access-before-approval hardens into a template — Merck runs Gilead's playbook
narratives.detail: Merck has issued voluntary licenses for its long-acting PrEP candidate alimatravir to low- and middle-income-country manufacturers ahead of any regulatory submission, following Gilead's lenacapavir sequence almost step for step. Two sponsors running the same pre-filing playbook starts to look less like goodwill and more like an emerging standard for long-acting prevention. The open question is whether it travels beyond HIV to other long-acting modalities.

narratives.headline: Biotech capital goes venue-shopping — Hong Kong listings and a Korean megadeal tilt the map east
narratives.detail: A US biotech is pursuing a Hong Kong-first IPO — a second alternative-venue data point after Scribe Therapeutics' upsized $128.7M Nasdaq debut — while Samsung Biologics moves on a roughly $1.8B acquisition billed as the largest ever by a Korean biopharma. With fresh US import tariffs now landing on generics too, the capital and supply-chain map is visibly leaning toward Asia. No single-asset thesis here, but the direction of travel is hard to miss.
